newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FIGURE SKATING-URMANOV NOW AT EASE WITH OLYMPIC TITLE.
newsitem.headline: FIGURE SKATING-URMANOV NOW AT EASE WITH OLYMPIC TITLE.

text.p: Alexei Urmanov believes he has finally come to terms with his status as Olympic men's figure skating champion - three years after winning the title at the Lillehammer Games in Norway.

Urmanov leads Russia's challenge against the dominant North American double act of titleholder Todd Eldredge and ex-champion Elvis Stojko as he attempts to add a first world title to his Olympic and European crowns.
Competition begins on Wednesday with the medals to be decided on Thursday night.
After winning his qualifying group on Sunday with a huge quadruple jump, the 23-year-old from St Petersburg reflected on his momentous achievement at the 1994 Winter Games.
"I was not ready to win the Olympic title. I didn't understand what the Olympic title was. I didn't understand the responsibility of being champion," he said.
"My friends would say to me 'Hey, you're the Olympic champion', and I didn't understand what it really meant. For a year I didn't understand."
What Urmanov, just 20 when he won the title, did realise quickly was that his success brought with it the huge expectations of the skating world.
"As the Olympic champion, I'm not allowed to fail," he once said.
Now he has come to terms with the demands of his status, his skating is enjoying a renaissance.
Though he was slightly fortunate to take the European title in a scrambled finish in Paris in January, he is skating better now than at any time since Lillehammer.
"I feel better than last season or the season before. I'm definitely going up," he said.
Urmanov and team mate Ilya Kulik, the 1995 European champion who also did a fine quad in qualifying, and Ukrainian Viacheslav Zagorodniuk offer the main opposition to Elfredge and Stojko.
Zagorodniuk, the European champion last year, did not do a quad but his triple axels are regarded as the best of the current skaters.
Eldredge and Stojko will both need to improve on their qualifying programmes.
The American champion rated his sprained right ankle at about 90 per cent on Sunday despite his fall on a triple axel late in his routine.
Stojko, who won the two world championships before Eldredge's success in Edmonton last year, tumbled landing his quad.

But he did not seem concerned and appeared confident he could repeat the magnificent quad-triple jump combination he brought off for the frirst time in the Champions Series final in Hamilton early this month.
With the Russians breathing down his neck, he may need to.
